labels.answer: Cooling area for sterile items awaiting storage
Items waiting to be in sterilizer

cloze.text: In an ultrasonic cleaner, process loose instruments for {{c1::1–15}} minutes and cassettes for {{c2::10–20}} minutes.
cloze.extra: Keep the unit covered during use.

cloze.text: Keep the ultrasonic cleaner {{c1::covered}} while it is running.
After ultrasonic cleaning, {{c1::rinse}} instruments thoroughly and allow them to {{c2::drain and dry}}.
To ensure full exposure in the ultrasonic cleaner, avoid {{c1::overloading}} the unit and {{c2::disassemble}} items.
The ultrasonic cleaner itself should be disinfected {{c1::daily}}.
If instruments must be hand scrubbed, use {{c1::heavy-duty}} gloves and {{c2::long-handled}} brushes.
{{c1::Automatic instrument washers}} use high-temperature cycles to clean and {{c2::thermally disinfect}} instruments, reducing manual handling.
The steam autoclave uses {{c1::moist heat under pressure}} to denature proteins and kill microbes.
Dry heat sterilization uses high dry heat to {{c1::oxidize}} and denature cell parts.
Unsaturated chemical vapor sterilization uses heated vapors of {{c1::alcohol + formaldehyde}} under pressure.
Steam autoclave cycles: 121°C for {{c1::20–30}} min, or 135°C for {{c2::3–10}} min.
Dry heat sterilizes at {{c1::162–180°C}}: {{c2::6–20 min}} in the rapid type or {{c3::1–2 hours}} in the oven type.
cloze.extra: Dry heat subtypes: rapid type and oven type.

cloze.text: Unsaturated chemical vapor sterilizes at {{c1::135°C}} for {{c2::20–30}} min.
Sterilizer pressures: steam autoclave {{c1::15–20 psi}}; unsaturated chemical vapor {{c2::20–40 psi}}; dry heat {{c3::none}}.
Steam autoclave subtypes: gravity displacement and {{c1::pre-vacuum}} (faster, deeper steam penetration).
Steam autoclave advantages: fast, reliable, and {{c1::wraps allowed}}.
Steam autoclave disadvantages: may {{c1::dull or corrode}} instruments, may {{c2::melt plastic}}, and needs {{c3::distilled water}}.
The {{c1::steam autoclave}} is the standard sterilizer in dental offices for general wrapped instruments.
Dry heat advantages: maintains {{c1::sharpness}}, prevents {{c2::corrosion}}, and uses no moisture.
Dry heat disadvantages: {{c1::longer cycles}}, damages {{c2::rubber/plastics}}, and special packaging may be needed.
Dry heat is ideal for {{c1::sharp instruments}} and {{c2::moisture-sensitive}} metal.
Unsaturated chemical vapor maintains sharpness and is {{c1::less corrosive}} than steam.
Unsaturated chemical vapor disadvantages: {{c1::chemical odor}} (ventilation needed) and may damage plastics/rubber.
Unsaturated chemical vapor is used for instruments sensitive to {{c1::steam or moisture}}.
{{c1::Formaldehyde}} is still used in some dental sterilizers, like {{c2::Chemiclaves}}, because it is effective at killing spores and viruses.
Cold sterilization is immersion in {{c1::EPA}}-approved chemical solutions.
Ethylene oxide sterilization uses {{c1::low-temperature}} ethylene oxide gas.
Flash sterilization uses the same temperatures as the steam autoclave ({{c1::121–135°C}}) for {{c2::3–10}} min at {{c3::15–20 psi}}.
Cold sterilization: {{c1::room temperature}}, often a {{c2::10+ hour}} soak, no pressure.
Ethylene oxide gas: 25°C (77°F) for {{c1::10–16}} hours in a {{c2::low-pressure}} sealed chamber.
Flash sterilization is a fast option for {{c1::emergencies}}, but no wrapping means {{c2::no sterile storage}} and risk of contamination.
cloze.extra: Flash, cold and ethylene oxide sterilization have no subtypes.

cloze.text: Cold sterilization can be used on some {{c1::heat-sensitive semi-critical}} items when heat sterilization isn't possible.
Cold sterilization requires a long soak and is NOT for {{c1::critical}} items and NOT for {{c2::single-use}} items.
Ethylene oxide is ideal for {{c1::plastic/rubber}} and other heat- and moisture-sensitive materials.
Ethylene oxide is very slow, expensive, and needs special equipment and ventilation, so it is used mainly in {{c1::hospitals}}, not typical dental practice.
{{c1::Mechanical}} monitoring uses built-in gauges, digital displays, or printouts on the sterilizer.
{{c1::Chemical}} monitoring uses color-changing indicators (tape, pouches, strips) that react to heat or sterilant.
{{c1::Biological}} monitoring (the spore test) uses paper strips or vials containing highly resistant {{c2::bacterial spores}}.
Mechanical monitoring checks {{c1::time, temperature, and pressure}}, showing the cycle ran correctly.
Chemical monitoring checks whether {{c1::physical conditions}} (e.g., temperature, time, sterilant) were met.
Biological monitoring checks whether actual {{c1::microorganisms are killed}}, proving sterilization occurred.
Mechanical monitoring: view the digital screen or pressure gauge {{c1::before and after}} the cycle; the clinician records it {{c2::immediately}}.
cloze.extra: Correct readings = cycle ran properly; abnormal readings = possible malfunction.

cloze.text: {{c1::Autoclave tape}} is placed outside packs and changes color (white to black) when heated.
cloze.extra: The figure caption describes indicator stripes changing from green to black; either way, the stripes darken.

cloze.text: {{c1::Internal}} chemical indicators are placed inside packs to confirm the sterilant reached the instruments.
Chemical indicator classes: Class {{c1::I}} = external (e.g., autoclave tape); Classes {{c2::II/IV/V}} = internal (single- or multi-parameter).
For a spore test, a spore strip is placed inside a pouch or cassette; some are {{c1::self-contained vials}} with growth media.
After sterilization, spore strips/vials are {{c1::incubated}} for {{c2::24 hours}} (in-office or mailed to a lab).
A chemical indicator's color change means conditions were met but is {{c1::not proof of sterility}}.
Spore test: if spores do {{c1::not grow}}, sterilization was effective; if spores {{c2::grow}}, sterilization failed.
Use mechanical monitoring on {{c1::every load}} and chemical indicators on {{c2::every pack or load}}, especially with internal instruments.
Besides weekly, spore test after sterilizer {{c1::repairs}}, with loads containing {{c2::implantable devices}}, and after new staff or new sterilizer use.
Mechanical and chemical monitoring results are immediate; biological results are delayed {{c1::24–48}} hours (faster in-office, slower by mail).
Biological monitoring systems: {{c1::in-office incubation kits}} (faster, more hands-on) or {{c2::mail-in services}} (convenient, slower).
cloze.extra: Mechanical monitoring is built into the sterilizer.

cloze.text: {{c1::Biological monitoring}} is the most accurate: the only method that proves microorganisms were destroyed.
Causes of sterilization failure: chamber {{c1::overload}}, excessive {{c2::packaging material}}, inadequate {{c3::exposure time}}, and incorrect temperature/pressure settings.
More causes of sterilization failure: failure to {{c1::preheat}} the sterilizer (if indicated), {{c2::interruption}} of the cycle, and {{c3::expired}} chemical solution.
Packages and cassettes should be placed on their {{c1::edges or vertically}}, not lying flat.
If mechanical and chemical indicators show the sterilizer works correctly, a single positive spore test does {{c1::not}} indicate sterilizer malfunction.
After a single positive spore test, items other than {{c1::implantable devices}} do not necessarily need recall; {{c2::repeat the spore test}} immediately after correctly loading the sterilizer.
If the repeated spore test is negative, return the sterilizer to service and re-challenge with spore tests in {{c1::three}} consecutive {{c2::empty-chamber}} cycles.
If the repeated spore test is positive, {{c1::remove the sterilizer from service}}. Record biologic monitoring results in a {{c2::logbook}}.
Use a {{c1::closed}} transportation box to move instruments to the processing area.
For instrument cleaning and decontamination, wear {{c1::puncture- and chemical-resistant heavy-duty utility}} gloves.
Clean debris by hand washing or an automated process: {{c1::ultrasonic cleaner}} or automatic washer.
After cleaning, rinse instruments with water to remove {{c1::chemical or detergent residue}}.
Wear puncture-resistant utility gloves when packaging instruments; utility gloves can be {{c1::disinfected or sterilized in an autoclave}}.
A chemical indicator should be used {{c1::inside every package}} to verify the sterilizing agent has penetrated the package and reached the instruments.
Add an {{c1::external}} chemical indicator (e.g., indicator tape) when the internal indicator cannot be seen from outside the package.
Chemical indicators differentiate {{c1::processed from unprocessed}} items, eliminating the possibility of using unsterilized instruments.
Arrange items to permit {{c1::free circulation}} of the sterilizing agent (steam, chemical vapor, or dry heat).
Instrument packs should be allowed to {{c1::dry}} inside the sterilizer chamber before they are removed.
Sterilization should be monitored by {{c1::mechanical}}, {{c2::chemical}}, and {{c3::biological}} indicators.
Boiling water ({{c1::100°C}}) does not destroy {{c2::bacterial spores}}.
cloze.extra: Did you know: once hepatitis B and HIV became concerns in the 1980s, autoclaves (up to 135°C under pressure) became the gold standard in dentistry.

cloze.text: The sterile storage area should be {{c1::enclosed}} and {{c2::dry}}.
Instruments should be {{c1::cooled}} before being stored.
Write the {{c1::date}} and the {{c2::sterilizer used}} on the packaging.
During radiographic exposure, use PPE if {{c1::blood or other bodily fluids}} are likely to contact the clinician.
Heat-tolerant radiograph items (e.g., receptor-holding and positioning devices) should be {{c1::heat-sterilized}}.
cloze.extra: The book says "film-holding" devices; the exam now says image receptor.

cloze.text: During radiography, {{c1::cover}} items likely to be contaminated: PID, tube head, swivel arms, countertop, keyboard, mouse, light handle, exposure control switch, headrest, chair controls.
After a sharps exposure, wash the injured area with antimicrobial {{c1::soap and water}}.
After an exposure, flush mucous membranes with {{c1::water}}.

Immediately {{c1::report}} an exposure to the {{c2::infection control coordinator}} (or designated person), who should initiate referral to the qualified health care professional and complete reports.
An exposure report records the {{c1::date and time}} of exposure and details of the {{c2::procedure}} being performed.
Exposure details in the report include {{c1::depth of injury}}, {{c2::type of instrument}} used, and {{c3::amount of blood}}.

The exposure report records whether the {{c1::source material}} was known to contain HIV or other blood-borne pathogens, details of the {{c2::exposed person}}, and counselling, {{c3::post-exposure management}}, and follow-up.
The first known provider-to-patient HIV transmission: Florida dentist {{c1::Dr. David Acer}} was linked to transmission to {{c2::six}} patients.
cloze.extra: It led to mandatory gloves and masks and the creation of standard precautions: treat every patient as potentially infectious.

cloze.text: Most bacteria are {{c1::harmless or beneficial}} (e.g., some strains of E. coli in the intestinal tract); only {{c2::pathogenic}} (disease-causing) bacteria are harmful.
{{c1::Streptococcus pyogenes}} causes streptococcal pharyngitis and {{c2::scarlet fever}}.
{{c1::Treponema pallidum}} causes {{c2::syphilis}}; spread by direct contact and {{c3::transplacental}}ly.
{{c1::Mycobacterium tuberculosis}} causes {{c2::tuberculosis}}; spread by {{c3::droplet nuclei}}, sputum, saliva.
Food poisoning is caused by {{c1::Escherichia coli}} and {{c2::Salmonella}}.
{{c1::Helicobacter pylori}} causes {{c2::gastritis and ulcers}}.
{{c1::Neisseria gonorrhoeae}} causes {{c2::gonorrhea}} (direct and indirect contact).
{{c1::Neisseria meningitidis}} causes {{c2::meningitis}}: inflammation of the meninges, the {{c3::three}} membranes covering the brain and spinal cord.
{{c1::Clostridium difficile}} causes {{c2::colitis}}.
Strep throat is caused by {{c1::Group A Streptococcus}} (respiratory droplets, direct contact).
{{c1::Cellulitis}} (a common, sometimes painful bacterial skin infection) is caused by {{c2::Staphylococcus}} and Streptococcus.
The STD chlamydia is caused by {{c1::Chlamydia trachomatis}}.
Viruses are {{c1::non-living}} organisms smaller than bacteria that require {{c2::living hosts}} (humans, plants, animals) to multiply.
AIDS is caused by the {{c1::human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)}}.
{{c1::Hepatitis D}} virus can only occur in the presence of {{c2::HBV}}.
Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis and recurrent herpes are both caused by {{c1::herpes simplex virus}}.
Hand, foot, and mouth disease is caused by {{c1::Coxsackie virus}}.
Infectious mononucleosis is caused by the {{c1::Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)}}.
Rubeola (measles) is from the {{c1::Paramyxoviridae}} family; rubella (German measles) is a {{c2::Togavirus}}.
cloze.extra: Both named for their reddish rashes: "rubeola" = little red, "rubella" = reddish (Latin). Different viruses, very different symptoms and risks.

cloze.text: Encephalitis and meningitis can be caused by {{c1::herpes virus}}.
Chickenpox is caused by {{c1::varicella zoster virus (VZV)}}.
Measles (rubeola) is caused by measles virus, genus {{c1::Morbillivirus}}; spread by direct contact, saliva, and {{c2::airborne droplet}}.
Mumps virus spreads by direct contact through saliva, droplets, and the {{c1::fecal-oral}} route.
Influenza viruses come in types {{c1::A, B, C}}; spread by nasal discharge and respiratory droplets.
Polio is caused by poliovirus types {{c1::1, 2, 3}}.
Ebola belongs to the viral family {{c1::Filoviridae}}.
Rabies virus is spread through the {{c1::saliva of infected animals}}.

cloze.section: Infectious agents transmissible from the oral cavity
cloze.text: Viruses transmissible from the oral cavity include HIV, HBV, HCV, {{c1::HEV}}, herpes simplex (types 1 and 2), {{c2::HPV}}, varicella zoster, Epstein-Barr, mumps, polio, influenza, measles, and rubella viruses.
cloze.extra: Note: the quiz answer key says HIV is not spread through saliva or aerosols in dental settings.

cloze.section: Infectious agents transmissible from the oral cavity
cloze.text: Bacteria and fungi transmissible from the oral cavity include M. tuberculosis, T. pallidum, N. gonorrhoeae, {{c1::Bordetella pertussis}}, Group A streptococci, Staphylococcus aureus and epidermidis, {{c2::Candida albicans}}, and Streptococcus pneumoniae.
Vaccines for healthcare workers: chickenpox (varicella), influenza, hepatitis B, {{c1::meningococcal}}, MMR, and Tdap.
The hepatitis B vaccine also protects against {{c1::hepatitis D}}.
MMR protects against {{c1::measles, mumps, and rubella}}; Tdap against {{c2::tetanus, diphtheria, and whooping cough}}.
Depending on local authorities, other vaccines may be required: HPV, {{c1::shingles}}, COVID-19, etc.
There is NO vaccine for {{c1::hepatitis C}} or {{c2::HIV}}.
The {{c1::CDC}} (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) is a federal {{c2::advisory}} agency that develops national infection prevention {{c3::guidelines}} for dental settings.
CDC key responsibilities: Standard Precautions, dental {{c1::waterlines}}, {{c2::post-exposure}} protocols, and outbreak guidance (e.g., COVID, TB).
The CDC does NOT {{c1::enforce laws, inspect offices, or approve products}}.
{{c1::NIOSH}} (National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health) is a federal {{c2::research}} agency that studies occupational health risks, e.g., in dental clinics.
NIOSH researches PPE, airborne diseases, and {{c1::latex allergies}}, but does NOT regulate or enforce rules.
{{c1::OSHA}} (Occupational Safety and Health Administration) is a federal {{c2::regulatory}} agency that enforces workplace safety laws for {{c3::employees}}.
OSHA covers the {{c1::Bloodborne Pathogens (BBP) Standard}}, exposure plans, PPE, disinfection, vaccination, sterilization, and {{c2::eyewash}}.
OSHA does NOT {{c1::write guidelines}} (like the CDC) or {{c2::approve products}}.
The {{c1::EPA}} (Environmental Protection Agency) is a federal regulatory agency that regulates {{c2::surface disinfectants}} and {{c3::medical waste}}.
The EPA approves disinfectants for environmental surfaces, monitors {{c1::drinking water}}, and handles waste (sharps, {{c2::amalgam}}).
The EPA does NOT approve {{c1::devices or patient-care instruments}}.
The {{c1::FDA}} (Food and Drug Administration) is a federal regulatory agency that regulates dental/medical {{c2::devices}} and {{c3::chemical sterilants}}.
The FDA approves gloves, masks, {{c1::sterilizers}}, indicators, radiography, and disinfectants for {{c2::instruments}}, but does NOT issue practice guidelines.
{{c1::OSAP}} (Organization for Safety, Asepsis, and Prevention) is a {{c2::non-profit educational}} organization offering infection control education and best practices.
OSAP gives guidance on sterilization, waterline safety, surface asepsis, and continuing education, but does NOT {{c1::regulate, inspect, or approve products}}.

basic.front: Why is hand scrubbing of instruments not recommended, and when may it be done?
basic.back: Increased risk of sharps injuries. Only when ultrasonic or automated methods are not available.

basic.front: Why must formaldehyde (chemical vapor) sterilizers be used in sealed, ventilated systems?
basic.back: Formaldehyde is a respiratory irritant and a probable carcinogen.
basic.extra: That's why most offices now prefer steam or dry heat sterilization.

basic.back: Steam used on unwrapped items for rapid sterilization

basic.front: Which sterilized packages are considered contaminated, and what do you do?
basic.back: Packages dropped on the floor, punctured, torn, or that look wet. Repackage and re-sterilize the instruments before use.
basic.extra: Always examine the packaging before opening it chairside.

basic.front: After a needlestick, should you squeeze the wound or apply an antiseptic?
basic.back: No. There is no evidence that antiseptics or expressing fluid by squeezing the wound reduces blood-borne pathogen transmission.

mcq.question: Which sterilizer is correctly matched with its cycle parameters?
options: A. Steam autoclave — 135°C for 3–10 min at 15–20 psi
B. Dry heat — 121°C for 20–30 min at 15–20 psi
C. Unsaturated chemical vapor — 162°C for 1–2 hrs with no pressure
D. Dry heat — 135°C for 20–30 min at 20–40 psi
mcq.answer: A. Steam autoclave — 135°C for 3–10 min at 15–20 psi
mcq.explanation: Steam autoclave: 121°C for 20–30 min or 135°C for 3–10 min at 15–20 psi. Dry heat runs at 162–180°C with no pressure; 135°C for 20–30 min at 20–40 psi is unsaturated chemical vapor.

mcq.question: A hygienist is choosing a sterilization method for plastic items that would melt in one unit and be damaged in another. Which statement is correct?
options: A. Steam autoclave is safe for plastics because it uses lower temperatures
B. Both steam autoclave and dry heat can damage plastics
C. Dry heat is preferred for plastics because it contains no moisture
D. Unsaturated chemical vapor never damages plastics or rubber
mcq.answer: B. Both steam autoclave and dry heat can damage plastics
mcq.explanation: Steam may melt plastic; dry heat damages rubber/plastics. Chemical vapor may also damage plastics/rubber, so D is false.

mcq.question: A heat-sensitive semi-critical item must be reprocessed in a dental office where heat sterilization isn't possible. Which method does the book recommend?
options: B. Cold sterilization (immersion in an EPA-approved chemical)
mcq.answer: B. Cold sterilization (immersion in an EPA-approved chemical)
mcq.explanation: Cold sterilization is used when heat sterilization isn't possible for semi-critical items (never critical or single-use items). Flash sterilization is still steam at 121–135°C, so it is not an option for heat-sensitive items.

mcq.question: Which sterilizer monitoring result is available only after a delay of 24–48 hours?
mcq.explanation: Spore tests must be incubated, so results take 24–48 hours (faster in-office, slower by mail). Mechanical and chemical results, including internal multi-parameter indicators, are immediate.

mcq.question: A routine weekly spore test is positive. Mechanical readings and chemical indicators for that load were normal, and no implants were processed. What should be done first?
options: A. Remove the sterilizer from service permanently
B. Recall every instrument processed since the last negative test
C. Repeat the spore test immediately after correctly loading the sterilizer
D. Ignore the result and retest next week
mcq.answer: C. Repeat the spore test immediately after correctly loading the sterilizer
mcq.explanation: With normal mechanical and chemical indicators, one positive spore test does not mean malfunction. Repeat it right away after loading correctly. Only implantable devices must be recalled. The sterilizer is removed from service only if the repeat test is also positive.

mcq.question: A child presents with fever, oral ulcers, and vesicles on the hands and feet. Which virus is the most likely cause?
mcq.explanation: Hand, foot and mouth disease is caused by Coxsackie virus. HSV causes primary herpetic gingivostomatitis and recurrent herpes, not lesions on the hands and feet.

mcq.question: A new dental hygienist asks which bloodborne infections she cannot be vaccinated against. Which pair is correct?
options: A. Hepatitis B and hepatitis D
D. Hepatitis D and hepatitis C
mcq.explanation: There is no vaccine for hepatitis C or HIV. The hepatitis B vaccine also protects against hepatitis D, because HDV only occurs with HBV.

mcq.question: A dental office wants to confirm that the product used to disinfect countertops and the dental chair is approved. Which agency approves it?
mcq.explanation: The EPA approves disinfectants for environmental surfaces. The FDA approves devices, sterilizers and disinfectants for instruments, not surface disinfectants.

mcq.question: All of the following are true of the CDC EXCEPT:
options: A. It develops national infection prevention guidelines for dental settings
B. It issues guidance on dental waterlines and post-exposure protocols
C. It inspects dental offices and enforces the Bloodborne Pathogens Standard
D. It is a federal advisory agency
mcq.answer: C. It inspects dental offices and enforces the Bloodborne Pathogens Standard
mcq.explanation: The CDC advises; it does not enforce laws, inspect offices or approve products. OSHA enforces the Bloodborne Pathogens Standard.

mcq.question: Which item is correctly paired with its required level of processing?
options: A. Radiographic receptor holder – Intermediate-level disinfection
B. X-ray tube head – Heat sterilization
C. Mouth mirror – Heat sterilization or high-level disinfection
D. Blood pressure cuff – High-level disinfection
mcq.answer: C. Mouth mirror – Heat sterilization or high-level disinfection
mcq.explanation: Mouth mirrors are semi-critical items that contact mucous membranes and must be either heat sterilized or high-level disinfected. Radiographic receptor holders are also semi-critical (same rule applies). X-ray tube heads and blood pressure cuffs are non-critical and only require low- or intermediate-level disinfection. (The book says "film holder"; the exam uses image receptor.)

mcq.question: You open a pack of sterilized instruments and notice that the external chemical tape has changed color, but the internal indicator shows no change. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: A. Use the instruments but record the incident.
B. Repeat the chemical test in the next load.
C. Consider the instruments unsterile and reprocess them.
D. Disregard the internal indicator; external is sufficient.
mcq.answer: C. Consider the instruments unsterile and reprocess them.
mcq.explanation: An external indicator only confirms that the package was exposed to sterilization conditions. Only the internal indicator confirms penetration of the sterilant. A failed internal indicator suggests that the instruments were not properly sterilized, and they must be reprocessed.

mcq.question: A sterilization pouch shows black lines on the tape but inside instruments are still contaminated. What does this suggest?
options: C. Only external indicators were used
mcq.answer: C. Only external indicators were used
mcq.explanation: External indicators (e.g., tape) only confirm exposure to heat. They do not confirm sterilant penetration. Internal indicators or biological monitoring are needed.

mcq.question: Which pathogen is not transmitted through saliva or aerosols in dental settings?
mcq.explanation: HIV is not spread through saliva or aerosols. In dental settings it spreads via blood, through needlesticks or mucosal exposure.

mcq.question: Which infection control principle is the foundation for treating all patients as potentially infectious?
mcq.explanation: Standard precautions assume all blood, saliva, and body fluids may carry infection, even in asymptomatic patients.

mcq.question: A dental unit waterline is flushed for only 5 seconds between patients. Which outcome is most likely?
options: B. Risk of biofilm transmission increases
mcq.answer: B. Risk of biofilm transmission increases
mcq.explanation: Inadequate flushing increases the risk of biofilm buildup and exposure to bacteria. Guidelines recommend 20–30 seconds between patients.

mcq.question: Which type of sterilization is best suited for maintaining sharp edges and avoiding corrosion in instruments?
mcq.explanation: Dry heat sterilization maintains the sharpness of instruments and does not cause corrosion, unlike moist heat.

mcq.question: Which of the following diseases requires airborne precautions (e.g., N95 respirator) during aerosol-generating dental procedures?
mcq.explanation: COVID-19 typically spreads by droplets, but during aerosol-generating procedures airborne precautions like N95 masks are required. The other options spread mainly by droplets.

mcq.question: In the chain of infection, what is the role of improperly canned food containing C. botulinum toxin?
mcq.explanation: The improperly canned food is a vehicle because it carries the toxin to the host. The actual reservoir is soil, where the organism naturally lives.

mcq.question: Which of the following statements about HIV transmission in dentistry is TRUE?
options: A. HIV is airborne and requires N95 use
B. HIV is commonly transmitted through saliva
C. Risk of HIV transmission after needlestick is approximately 0.3%
D. HIV survives on surfaces for 30 days
mcq.answer: C. Risk of HIV transmission after needlestick is approximately 0.3%
mcq.explanation: The risk of HIV transmission after a needlestick from HIV+ blood is about 0.3%. HIV is not airborne and does not spread through saliva.
